blocks.html: Every drawing starts with a line. A line is the mark your crayon makes when it moves across the paper.
Some lines go one way and never bend. They are straight. Some lines bend, like a smile or a rainbow. They are curved.

blocks.name: ar-lines

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A straight line and a curved line.

blocks.html: A straight line does not bend. A curved line bends.
When you know the names of lines, you can see them everywhere: the straight edge of a door, the curved top of an apple. Artists look for these lines and draw them.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Is the top of a rainbow straight or curved?
steps: Picture a rainbow in the sky.
It bends like a bridge.
A line that bends is curved.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Trace the dotted lines with your finger, then with a crayon. Print the sheet to trace on paper.

blocks.html: A straight line drawn by hand wobbles a little, and that is fine. It is still straight if you meant it to go one way. A curved line bends on purpose.
For the grown-up. Go on a line hunt around the house: the straight edge of a table, the curved handle of a cup. Let your child trace each one in the air.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Straight lines can point different ways. Stand up tall like a tree: that is a vertical line. Lie down flat like you are in bed: that is a horizontal line. Lean over like a slide: that is a diagonal line.

blocks.name: ar-lines

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines.

blocks.html: Vertical stands up. Horizontal lies down. Diagonal leans.
Horizontal comes from horizon, the flat line far away where the sky meets the land or the sea. Horizontal lines lie flat like the horizon.

blocks.name: ar-lines
blocks.cap: A flagpole stands up (vertical), the sea meets the sky in a flat line (horizontal), and a slide leans (diagonal).

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: The rungs of a ladder go across. Are they vertical or horizontal?
steps: The rungs lie flat, from one side to the other.
Lines that lie flat are horizontal.

blocks.name: ar-lines

opts.task: Tap the line that leans, then tap Check.

blocks.cap: Find the diagonal line.

blocks.html: Many people mix up vertical and horizontal. Use your body to remember: stand up for vertical, lie down for horizontal.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Lines can dance! A zigzag line goes up and down with sharp points, like teeth. A wavy line goes up and down with smooth bumps, like water. A spiral winds around and around, like a snail shell.

blocks.name: ar-lines

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A zigzag line, a wavy line and a spiral.

blocks.html: Zigzag lines have sharp points. Wavy lines have smooth bumps. Spirals go around and around.
Different lines make us feel different things. Zigzags look fast and sharp, like lightning. Wavy lines look calm and flowing, like the sea.

blocks.name: ar-lines
blocks.cap: Lightning zigzags, waves are wavy, and a snail shell is a spiral.

blocks.html: Zigzag and wavy lines both go up and down, so they are easy to mix up. Look at the tops: sharp corners make a zigzag; smooth, round bumps make a wavy line.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What kind of line does the edge of a row of pointy mountains make?
steps: The mountains go up to sharp tops and down again.
Sharp points make a zigzag.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Trace each dotted line. Then draw your own zigzag, wave and spiral.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: The same crayon can make different lines. Press gently and the line is thin and light. Press harder and the line is thick and dark. A fat marker makes thicker lines than a sharp pencil.

blocks.name: ar-lines

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Thin, thick, light and dark lines.

blocks.html: Gentle pressing makes light, thin lines. Harder pressing makes dark, thick lines.
Artists start with light lines because light lines are easy to erase. When the drawing looks right, they go over the best lines to make them darker.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw one line pressing gently, and one line pressing hard. With a pen or a tablet stylus, the line gets thicker as you press harder.

blocks.cap: Try gentle and hard lines.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Mia wants to draw a house she might change later. Should she start with light lines or dark lines?
steps: She might want to change it.
Light lines are easy to erase.

blocks.html: Pressing hard on every line makes every line look the same, and the lines are hard to erase. Start light; press harder only at the end.
For the grown-up. Hand your child a pencil and ask for the lightest line they can make, then the darkest. Make a little row from light to dark together.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Lines are not only in drawings. They are all around us! A ladder has straight lines. Waves on the water make wavy lines. A snail shell has a spiral.

blocks.name: ar-lines

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Lines in the world. The colored lines show the kind of line in each picture.

blocks.html: Artists look for lines in the things they see, then draw those lines.
When you can name the line, drawing it gets easier. A fence is just vertical lines with horizontal lines across them.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Rain blows in the wind. What kind of lines do the raindrops make?
steps: The rain does not fall straight down; the wind pushes it.
Lines that lean are diagonal.

blocks.name: ar-lines

opts.task: Tap the picture with a spiral, then tap Check.

blocks.cap: Find the spiral.

blocks.html: Some children look for lines only on paper. Look at real things too: edges, stripes, cracks and the folds in a shirt are all lines.
For the grown-up. On a walk, play "I spy a line": a zigzag on a roof, a wavy line in a puddle, a straight line along the curb.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: When a line goes all the way around and meets itself, it makes a shape. Three shapes help us draw almost anything: the circle, the square and the triangle.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A circle has no corners. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 corners. A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.

blocks.html: Count the corners: a circle has 0, a triangle has 3, and a square has 4.
Big drawings are made of simple shapes. A house is a square with a triangle on top. A snowman is three circles.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: A house, one shape at a time. Tap Next.

blocks.html: When a square is turned on its corner, some children think it is a new shape. Turning a shape does not change it: it still has 4 equal sides and 4 corners.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: Both of these are squares. The second one is just turned.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: How many corners does a triangle have?
steps: Touch each corner and count: one, two, three.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Trace the triangle. Then try a circle and a square of your own.

blocks.html: The Math Ladder's Kindergarten course has more about naming and building flat shapes.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: You know the circle, the square and the triangle. Now meet their friends! Stretch a square and it becomes a rectangle. Stretch a circle and it becomes an oval, like an egg.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A rectangle, an oval, a diamond, a star, a heart and a half circle.

blocks.html: A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides. An oval is a stretched circle. Diamonds, stars, hearts and half circles are shapes too.
The more shapes you know, the more things you can draw. A door is a rectangle. An egg is an oval. A kite is a diamond.

blocks.name: ydraw-things
blocks.cap: A door (rectangle), an egg (oval), a kite (diamond) and a slice of watermelon (half circle).

blocks.html: Many children call every shape with four sides a square. Look at the sides: in a square they are all the same length. A rectangle has two long sides and two short sides.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: A square and a rectangle. Run a finger along each side and compare.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: A book has two long sides and two short sides. What shape is it?
steps: Count the sides: 4.
Two are long and two are short.
That is a rectangle.

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Trace the star. Then try an oval and a heart on your own.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Hunt for rectangles and ovals at home: a phone, a rug, a mirror, a plate seen from the side. Ask, "Are all the sides the same, or are two of them longer?" The Math Ladder's What Makes a Shape a Shape goes further.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Here is an artist's trick. Before you draw something, look at it and ask: what shapes do I see? A clock is a circle. A slice of pizza is a triangle. A door is a rectangle.

blocks.name: ydraw-things

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Things with plain shapes: a clock, a slice of pizza, a door, an egg, a kite and a window.

blocks.html: Find the shapes first. Then draw the shapes.
A whole car looks hard to draw. But a car is only rectangles and circles. When you see the shapes, a hard drawing turns into a few easy ones.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: A car made of shapes: 2 rectangles, 2 squares and 2 circles.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What shapes would you use for a snowman?
steps: A snowman is three round snowballs.
Round shapes are circles.
Big at the bottom, smaller in the middle, smallest on top.

blocks.html: Some children draw the idea of a thing, like a "car" they remember, instead of the shapes in front of them. Name the shapes out loud first: "a long rectangle, a short rectangle, two circles." Then draw them.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: An owl, one shape at a time. Tap Next.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Play "What shapes?" at the table: a plate (circle), a napkin (square), a sandwich cut in half (two triangles). Let your child trace each shape in the air before drawing it.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work)

blocks.html: Some shapes are neat. Their sides are straight, or their curves are even, like a circle, a square or a triangle. Artists call these geometric shapes.
Other shapes are free. Their edges curve and wander in uneven ways, like a cloud, a leaf or a puddle. Artists call these organic shapes, because many of them come from nature.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Three neat shapes and three free shapes.

blocks.html: Neat (geometric) shapes have straight sides or even curves. Free (organic) shapes curve in uneven ways.
Most things people build, like boxes and windows, have neat shapes. Most things in nature, like rocks and leaves, have free shapes. Knowing the difference helps your drawings look right.
Some children think a shape needs a name, like "circle," to be a shape. When a line goes all the way around and meets itself, it makes a shape. A puddle is a shape too: a free one.

blocks.name: ar-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the shapes. Tap a card, then tap a group.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Is a pebble a neat shape or a free shape?
steps: A pebble is lumpy and a little uneven.
Its edge is not straight or perfectly round.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a neat shape, like a square. Then draw a free shape, like a cloud or a puddle.

blocks.cap: Draw one of each.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Take a "shape walk" outside. Point to a free shape (a cloud, a leaf) and a neat one (a window, a sign). Ask which is which and why.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Let's draw a house, one shape at a time. The walls are a big square. The roof is a triangle on top. The door is a tall rectangle, and the windows are little squares.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A house, one shape at a time. Tap Next.

blocks.html: Draw the big shapes first: walls, then roof. Add the small things, like the door and the windows, last.
Big shapes decide how much room your drawing takes. If you start with the big walls, everything else fits inside them. If you start with a tiny doorknob, you have to guess where the rest goes.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: You have drawn the walls. What comes next?
steps: The roof is the next biggest shape.
It sits on top of the walls, so draw a triangle there.
After that come the door and the windows.
blocks.a: The roof: a triangle on top.

blocks.html: Some children start with the small things, like the doorknob, and run out of room for the house. Big shapes first; details last.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.printTitle: Trace a house made of shapes

blocks.cap: Trace the house. Then draw your own house next to it: maybe two windows, maybe a chimney.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. After tracing, ask your child to draw the house again without the dotted lines, saying each shape aloud: "big square, triangle, rectangle." Then let them add their own touches, like a chimney, a path or a cat in the window.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A cat is made of easy shapes too. Start with a big oval for the body. Add a circle for the head. Put two triangles on top for the ears. Finish with a curved line for the tail.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A cat, one shape at a time. Tap Next.

blocks.html: Body oval, head circle, triangle ears, curved tail. The body is bigger than the head.
Real cats have a long body and a smaller head. When you get the sizes right, your cat looks like a cat, even with simple shapes.
Many children draw the head and the body the same size, or make the head bigger. Look at a real cat: its body is much bigger than its head.

blocks.name: ydraw-oops
blocks.cap: Which cat looks right? Compare the head with the body.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What shapes make the cat's ears?
steps: Ears are pointy at the top.
A shape with three sides and a point is a triangle.
A cat has two ears.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.printTitle: Trace a cat made of shapes

blocks.cap: Trace the cat. Then draw a cat of your own: sleeping, sitting, or with stripes.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. If you have a pet or a stuffed animal, look at it together and ask, "Which is bigger, the head or the body?" Then try drawing it from shapes.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A fish is an oval body with a triangle tail on the back end. Add a circle eye at the front and a little triangle fin on top.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A fish, one shape at a time. Tap Next.

blocks.html: A bird has an oval body and a circle head. Give it a small triangle beak, a curved line for the wing and a triangle tail.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: A bird, one shape at a time. Tap Next.

blocks.html: Fish: oval body, triangle tail at the back end, eye at the front. Bird: oval body, circle head, triangle beak.
The eye and the tail tell us which way an animal is facing. The eye goes at the front, where it is going. The tail goes at the back.
Some children put the fish's tail on the same end as the eye. Put the eye near the front and the tail on the other end.

blocks.name: ydraw-oops
blocks.cap: One fish has its tail in the right place.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Where does the bird's beak go?
steps: The beak is part of the face.
It goes on the head, at the front, next to the eye.
blocks.a: On the front of the head.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.printTitle: Trace a fish made of shapes

blocks.cap: Trace the fish. Then draw a bird of your own.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Draw a pond or a sky together, and let your child fill it with fish or birds facing different ways. Ask, "Which way is this one swimming?"

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Cars and trains are made of rectangles and circles. A car has a long rectangle body, a shorter rectangle on top, square windows and two circle wheels.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A car, one shape at a time. Tap Next.

blocks.html: A train engine has a tall rectangle cab, a long rectangle boiler, a little rectangle chimney and three circle wheels.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: A train engine made of shapes, with its parts named.

blocks.html: Rectangles for the body, circles for the wheels. The wheels sit at the bottom and touch the ground.
Wheels roll on the road. If they float up inside the car, the car looks like it is flying, not driving.
Many children draw the wheels inside the car, or floating above the road. Draw the road line first, then set the wheels on it.

blocks.name: ydraw-oops
blocks.cap: Which car's wheels touch the road?

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: How many circles does the train engine need?
steps: Count the wheels in the picture: one, two, three.
Each wheel is a circle.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.printTitle: Trace a car made of shapes

blocks.cap: Trace the car. Then draw a bus or a truck: more rectangles, more wheels.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Look at real cars on a walk and count the wheels you can see from the side (usually two). Ask, "Where do the wheels touch?"

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A tree is a tall rectangle trunk with a big, bumpy cloud of leaves on top. The leaves are a free shape, like the ones in Neat Shapes and Free Shapes.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A tree: a trunk and a cloud of leaves.

blocks.html: A flower starts with a circle in the middle. Put petals all the way around the circle, then add a long stem and a leaf.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: A flower made of shapes: a circle center, oval petals, a rectangle stem and an oval leaf.

blocks.html: Tree: rectangle trunk, bumpy leaves on top. Flower: circle center, petals all the way around, then a stem.
Petals grow in a ring around the middle of a flower. When you draw the center first, it is easy to fit the petals around it.
Some children draw all the petals on one side, or make them every different size. Go around the center like a clock, making the petals about the same size.

blocks.name: ydraw-oops
blocks.cap: Which flower has its petals all the way around?

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What do you draw first for a flower?
steps: The center is the middle of the flower.
The petals go around it, so it comes first.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.printTitle: Trace a flower made of shapes

blocks.cap: Trace the flower. Then draw a whole garden.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Look at a real flower together and count its petals before drawing it. Some have 5, some have many more.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: When one thing is in front of another, it hides part of the thing behind it. A ball in front of a box hides part of the box.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: In A, the ball is in front of the box. In B, both are drawn whole, so they look see-through.

blocks.html: Draw the front thing whole. Stop the lines of the thing behind it where the front thing begins.
Our eyes can't see through a ball. So in a drawing, the lines of the box disappear behind the ball. That is how a drawing shows which thing is closer to us.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: A tree stands in front of a house. Which one do you draw whole?
steps: The tree is in front.
The front thing is drawn whole.
Draw the house's lines up to the tree, then stop.

blocks.html: Many children draw every shape whole, so the box's lines show right through the ball. Draw the front thing first; then draw the back thing only where you can see it.

blocks.name: ydraw-scene
blocks.cap: The bush hides part of the tree, and the tree hides part of the house.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a big ball. Then draw a box behind it: stop the box's lines where they reach the ball.

blocks.cap: Try it: one thing in front of another.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Stack two cups so one is in front of the other and look from the side. Ask, "Can you see the whole back cup?" Then draw only what you can see.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: After rain, when the sun comes out behind you, you may see a rainbow. Its colors always come in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet (violet is a kind of purple).

blocks.name: ar-wheel

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A rainbow: red on the outside edge, violet on the inside.

blocks.html: A rainbow goes red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, with red on the outside edge.
Sunlight looks white, but it is made of all these colors mixed together. Raindrops spread the light out, and the colors always line up in the same order.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Which color comes right after yellow in a rainbow?
steps: Say the order: red, orange, yellow...
The next color is green.

blocks.html: Some children color a rainbow in any order. A real rainbow never changes its order. Start with red on the outside and work your way in.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: One band is missing. Which color goes there? (Green.)

blocks.name: ar-canvas
blocks.cap: Trace the curves, then draw your own rainbow in the right order.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. A handy way to remember the order is a made-up name, "Roy G. Biv" (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet). Many older books list indigo, a deep blue-violet, between blue and violet; this course keeps six colors for young eyes.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Painters have three very special colors: red, yellow and blue. They are called the primary colors. "Primary" means "first."

blocks.name: ar-wheel

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: The painter's three primary colors: red, yellow and blue.

blocks.html: In paint, the primary colors are red, yellow and blue.
With red, yellow and blue paint, you can mix many other colors, like orange, green and purple. That is why painters call them the first colors.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Is green a primary color in paint?
steps: The primaries are red, yellow and blue.
Green is not one of them.
Green can be mixed from yellow and blue.

blocks.html: Many children think green is a primary color in paint. Green paint can be mixed from yellow and blue, so it is not a primary.

blocks.name: ar-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the paint colors.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. This course uses the painter's traditional primaries (red, yellow, blue), which work well for children's paints. Printers use cyan, magenta and yellow, and screens use red, green and blue light; the Color and Design course explains all three.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Now the fun part: mixing! Put two primary colors together and you get a new color, called a secondary color.

blocks.name: ar-wheel

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Red and yellow make orange. Try other pairs.

blocks.html: Red + yellow = orange. Yellow + blue = green. Red + blue = purple.
Each secondary color sits between the two colors that make it. Orange is a little like red and a little like yellow.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Ruby wants to paint a green frog but has no green paint. What can she do?
steps: Green is made from two primaries.
Yellow and blue make green.
She mixes yellow and blue.

blocks.html: If you stir every color together, you get a muddy brown. Mix only two colors at a time, and rinse your brush before you change colors.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: The six colors: the primaries, with the secondary colors in between.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. With three small cups of paint (red, yellow, blue) and a paper plate, your child can make all three secondary colors. A drop of yellow first, then a little blue, is easier to control than the other way around, because blue is strong.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Some colors look warm, like a fire or the sun: red, orange and yellow. Some colors look cool, like water, sky and leaves: blue, green and purple.

blocks.name: ar-wheel

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Warm colors on one side of the wheel, cool colors on the other.

blocks.html: Warm: red, orange, yellow. Cool: blue, green, purple.
We call them warm and cool because of the things they remind us of. A fire is red and orange. The sea and the shade under trees are blue and green.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Omar is painting a snowy night. Should he use mostly warm or cool colors?
steps: Snow and night feel cold.
Cool colors look like water, ice and shade.
blocks.a: Mostly cool colors, like blues and purples.

blocks.html: Some children think warm colors are the colors they like best. Warm and cool are about fire and sun versus water and leaves, not about favorites. Your favorite color can be warm or cool.

blocks.name: ar-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the colors into warm and cool.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Make two quick pictures together: a campfire using only warm crayons, and a pond using only cool ones. Ask which one looks hot and which looks cold.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: You can change a color without changing what color it is. Add white and it gets lighter: red becomes pink. Add a tiny bit of black and it gets darker: red becomes dark red.

blocks.name: ar-value

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Blue from light (lots of white) to dark (a little black).

blocks.html: White makes a color lighter. Black makes a color darker. Add black just a little at a time.
White paint is the lightest paint there is, and black is the darkest. Mixing in a little of either moves a color toward light or dark.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Hana wants light blue for the sky. What should she add to her blue paint?
steps: Light blue is lighter than blue.
White makes a color lighter.

blocks.html: Many children add a big blob of black, and the color turns almost black. Black is very strong: add a tiny bit, stir, and look before you add more.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Red with more and more white: from red to pale pink.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Green with more and more black: from green to very dark green.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. On a paper plate, put a spot of one color and make a row: plain, plus a little white, plus more white. Then try a second row with the tiniest touch of black. Your child will see how strong black is.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A color wheel puts the colors in a circle: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, and back to red. Each secondary color sits between the two colors that make it.

blocks.name: ar-wheel

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A six-color wheel.

blocks.html: Colors across from each other are opposites: red and green, yellow and purple, blue and orange.
Opposite colors sit straight across the wheel. Side by side, they make each other look bright.
Put red next to green and both look stronger. Artists use opposites to make part of a picture pop, like a red apple among green leaves.

blocks.name: ar-wheel
blocks.cap: Tap a color to find its opposite.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What is the opposite of blue?
steps: Put your finger on blue.
Go straight across the middle of the wheel.
You land on orange.

blocks.html: Some children think opposite colors "don't go together." Opposites side by side look bright and lively; that is why artists like them. (Mixed together in paint, though, they make a dull brown.)
For the grown-up. Look for opposites in picture books, flags and sports uniforms: a red bird on a green branch, an orange fish in blue water. Ask your child which color makes the other look brighter.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A pattern repeats the same part again and again. Red circle, blue square, red circle, blue square... The part that repeats is "red circle, blue square."

blocks.name: ydraw-row

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A pattern: red circle, blue square, again and again.

blocks.html: Find the part that repeats. Then keep repeating it the same way.
Patterns are everywhere: on clothes, wallpaper, quilts and floors. Artists use patterns to decorate and to make a picture feel even and calm.

blocks.name: ydraw-row
blocks.cap: Row A is a pattern (star, heart, heart). Row B never repeats.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What is the part that repeats in star, heart, heart, star, heart, heart?
steps: Say it out loud: star, heart, heart... star, heart, heart.
It starts over after the second heart.

blocks.html: Some children repeat the part once and then change the rule. Say the pattern out loud as you draw, and point to each piece.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Make a pattern in the boxes: for example, circle, triangle, circle, triangle.

blocks.cap: Make your own pattern.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Clap a pattern (clap, clap, stomp; clap, clap, stomp) and ask your child to keep it going. Then turn it into colors or shapes on paper. The next topic turns this into a game.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: If you know the part that repeats, you can tell what comes next. Look at the whole part, not only the last piece.

blocks.name: ar-pattern

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Circle, triangle, triangle... what comes next? Tap a piece.

blocks.html: Say the pattern out loud. Find where it starts over. Then the next piece is easy.
A pattern is a rule. Once you know the rule, you can keep it going forever.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, ? What comes next?
steps: The part that repeats is red, blue, blue.
After red comes blue.

blocks.html: Many children guess from the last piece only. In red, blue, blue, red, blue, ? someone looking only at the last blue might say red, because red came after a blue before. But the part that repeats is red, blue, blue, so the next piece is blue.

blocks.name: ydraw-row
blocks.cap: Which piece comes next? (B: a green circle.)

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Make bead or snack patterns (cereal, crackers, grapes) and leave a gap for your child to fill. Then swap: your child makes the pattern and you guess.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: People are not the only pattern makers. Nature makes patterns too! A zebra has stripes. A leopard has spots. A fish has scales. A snail shell has a spiral.

blocks.name: ar-pattern

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Patterns in nature: stripes, spots, scales, a spiral, a honeycomb's six-sided cells and a tree stump's rings.

blocks.html: Stripes, spots, scales, spirals and rings are patterns in nature.
Patterns help animals and plants. Stripes and spots can help an animal hide in grass or shade. A honeycomb's six-sided cells fit together with no gaps.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What pattern do you see on a ladybug?
steps: A ladybug is red with round black marks.
Round marks are spots.

blocks.html: Some children think only people make patterns. Look closely at animals and plants: zebras, snails, pinecones, fish and sunflowers are full of them.

blocks.name: ar-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the animals by their pattern.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw an animal and give it a pattern: stripes, spots or scales.

blocks.cap: Draw a patterned animal.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. On a walk or in a picture book, look for patterns: bark, leaves, shells, feathers. Ask, "What repeats here?"

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Fold a paper butterfly down the middle: the two wings match! When one half is a mirror picture of the other half, the thing is symmetrical.

blocks.name: ar-pattern

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Half a butterfly. Tap the button to show the mirror half.

blocks.html: Symmetrical means the two halves match like a mirror. The mirror half faces the other way.
Many living things are close to symmetrical: butterflies, leaves, faces. When you draw one side, the other side mirrors it.
Many children copy the half instead of flipping it, so both halves point the same way. A mirror half faces the other way, like your left hand and your right hand.

blocks.name: ar-pattern
blocks.cap: In A the right half is a mirror picture. In B the half was copied without flipping.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Is the letter A symmetrical?
steps: Picture a line straight down the middle of A.
The left slant and the right slant match like a mirror.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw on one side of the dotted line. The pad draws the mirror half for you.

blocks.cap: A mirror drawing pad: whatever you draw is mirrored on the other side.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Fold a paper in half, paint blobs on one side, fold and press: you get a symmetrical "butterfly print." Older children can explore lines of symmetry in the Math Ladder's Lines of Symmetry.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Touch your own face. Your eyes are about halfway between the top of your head and your chin. Your nose is below your eyes, and your mouth is below your nose. Your ears are on the sides.

blocks.name: ydraw-face

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: The dashed line is halfway down the head. The eyes sit right on it.

blocks.html: Eyes about halfway down. Then the nose. Then the mouth. Ears on the sides.
Above the eyes there is a whole forehead, and the hair sits on top of that. That is why the eyes are lower than most people expect.
Many children put the eyes near the very top of the head, leaving no room for a forehead. Draw a light line halfway down, and put the eyes on it.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: In B the eyes are about halfway down. In A they are too high.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What goes between the eyes and the mouth?
steps: From the top: eyes, then nose, then mouth.
The nose is in the middle of the three.

blocks.name: ydraw-face
blocks.cap: Each face is missing one part. Can you name it?

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a face on the guide lines: eyes on the halfway line, then the nose and the mouth.

blocks.cap: Draw a face with the guide lines.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Look in a mirror together and measure with fingers: top of the head to the eyes, eyes to the chin. They are about the same.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: A face can show how someone feels. Look at the mouth. A mouth that curves up looks happy. A mouth that curves down looks sad. A round, open mouth looks surprised.

blocks.name: ydraw-face

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A: happy. B: sad. C: surprised.

blocks.html: Mouth up: happy. Mouth down: sad. Mouth a round O: surprised.
When we feel something, the muscles in our face move. Artists copy those shapes, so we can tell how a person in a picture feels.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: Tap a feeling and watch the face change.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Leo's ice cream fell on the ground. How might his mouth look?
steps: Losing an ice cream feels sad.
A sad mouth curves down.
blocks.a: Curved down, like a sad face.

blocks.html: Some children draw every face with the same smile, even when the story is sad. Choose the mouth to match the feeling.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw three circles. Give one a happy mouth, one a sad mouth and one a surprised mouth.

blocks.cap: Draw three feelings.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Play "make a face": you name a feeling and your child makes it in a mirror, then draws it. Talk about a time each feeling happened.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Grades 1 to 3 (Connecting: relate artistic ideas and works to personal meaning)

blocks.html: Eyebrows talk too! Raised eyebrows, up high, look surprised. Eyebrows that slope down toward the nose look cross (angry). Eyebrows that tilt up in the middle look worried.

blocks.name: ydraw-face

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: The same mouth, three feelings: A surprised, B cross, C worried.

blocks.html: The eyebrows show a feeling as much as the mouth does.
Look at the three faces: only the eyebrows changed, yet each face feels different. A few short lines above the eyes can change a whole drawing.
Many children change only the mouth. Try changing the eyebrows too: a cross face with a smile looks mixed up.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Mia wants to draw a surprised face. How should the eyebrows look?
steps: When we are surprised, our eyebrows jump up.
Draw them high above the eyes, curved up.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: Look at the eyebrows on each face.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw two faces with the same mouth. Give one raised eyebrows and one eyebrows that slope down.

blocks.cap: Change only the eyebrows.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. In front of a mirror, keep your mouths still and move only your eyebrows: up, down, tilted. Ask your child which feeling each one shows.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Grades 1 to 3 (Connecting: relate artistic ideas and works to personal meaning)

blocks.html: You can build a whole person from shapes! A circle for the head. A rectangle for the body. Two long shapes for the arms, starting at the shoulders. Two long shapes for the legs. Then add a face, hair, hands and shoes.

blocks.name: ydraw-person

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A person, one shape at a time. Tap Next.

blocks.html: Head, body, arms, legs: big shapes first. The arms start at the shoulders.
Our arms join our bodies at the shoulders, at the top corners of the body. Starting them there makes your person look like they could wave.
Many children attach the arms to the head. Touch your own shoulders: that is where your arms begin.

blocks.name: ydraw-person
blocks.cap: In A, the arms start at the shoulders. In B, they come out of the head.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: How many long shapes do you need for the arms and legs?
steps: Two arms and two legs.

blocks.name: ydraw-person
blocks.cap: The parts of a person: head, body, arms and legs.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a person from shapes: circle head, rectangle body, then arms and legs.

blocks.cap: Your turn.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Ask your child to stand like a star, arms out. Point to the shoulders, elbows and hips. Then draw the person from shapes together.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Once you can draw a person from shapes, make each person different! Change the hair: short, long, curly or in a ponytail. Add a hat or glasses. Choose clothes: pants, shorts or a skirt, in any color.

blocks.name: ydraw-person

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Four people, each one different: hair, hats, glasses, clothes and size.

blocks.html: Hair, hats, glasses, clothes and size show who is who.
In a picture of a family or a class, everyone needs to look like themselves. Small changes make each person easy to find.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Which person in the picture wears a sun hat?
steps: Look at the tops of the heads.
Person D has a wide straw hat.

blocks.html: Some children draw everyone exactly the same. Change at least one thing for each person: the hair, the clothes, the size or the glasses.

blocks.name: ar-face
blocks.cap: A grandparent with gray hair and glasses.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw two people from your family. Make them different with hair, clothes, hats or glasses.

blocks.cap: Draw your people.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Ask your child to draw your family and tell you how they will show who is who: a beard, a favorite hat, a striped shirt, long braids.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Your paper is a stage, and the main thing in your picture is the star of the show. Draw it big, so it fills the page, not tiny in a corner.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: In A, the house is tiny in a corner. In B, it fills the page.

blocks.html: Make the main thing big. It is fine if it touches the edges of the paper.
A big drawing has room for details: windows, a cat on the step, flowers by the door. A tiny drawing leaves no room, and the empty paper takes over the picture.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Sam wants to draw his dog. How big should he draw it?
steps: The dog is the main thing in the picture.
The main thing should fill most of the page.
blocks.a: Big, filling most of the page.

blocks.html: Many children draw a tiny picture in one corner and leave the rest of the page empty. Before you start, point to where the top and the bottom of your drawing will go.

blocks.name: ydraw-scene
blocks.cap: A tiny tree and a tree that fills the page.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw one thing you love, as big as the pad. Let it touch the edges.

blocks.cap: Draw it big.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Before drawing, ask your child to put a finger where the top of the drawing will be and another where the bottom will be. Planning the size first is a habit real artists use.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: In a picture outside, the ground goes along the bottom of the page. The sky goes above it, all the way down to the ground.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: In A, the sky is a thin strip at the top, with white air below. In B, the sky comes all the way down.

blocks.html: The sky reaches all the way down to where the land ends. There is no white gap.
Look out a window: the sky does not stop high above the trees. It goes all the way down to the far-off line where the land meets the sky. That line is called the horizon.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Mia painted the grass at the bottom and a strip of blue at the top. What should go in the white part between?
steps: Outside, there is no white strip of air.
The sky comes down to the land.

blocks.html: Many children paint a thin strip of blue at the top, with white paper between the sky and the ground. Bring the sky color all the way down to the ground line.

blocks.name: ydraw-scene
blocks.cap: Sky down to the ground, ground along the bottom.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a ground line near the bottom. Color the ground below it and the sky all the way down to it.

blocks.cap: Your turn: sky and ground.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. On a walk, stop and look at the horizon together. Ask, "Where does the sky stop?" Then color a picture with the sky meeting the land.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Things that are far away look smaller, and they sit higher on the page. Things that are near look bigger, and they sit lower.

blocks.name: ydraw-scene

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A near tree, big and low, and a far tree and house, small and high.

blocks.html: Far: smaller and higher up the page. Near: bigger and lower.
Hold your hand up near your eye: it can cover a whole house far away. Near things fill more of what we see, so they look bigger.
Many children draw a faraway tree as big as a near one, side by side at the bottom of the page. Make the far tree smaller and move it up toward the horizon.

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: In A, the far things are smaller and higher. In B, the trees are the same size, so neither looks far away.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Leo draws a mountain far away and a flower right in front. Which should be bigger on his page?
steps: The flower is near.
Near things look bigger, even if they are small in real life.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw one big tree near the bottom and two small trees higher up, far away.

blocks.cap: Draw near and far.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Look down a street together: compare a car close by with one far away. Ask, "Which looks bigger? Which is higher up in what we see?"

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Artists have a secret: they look a lot. When you draw something real, like a cup, a shoe or a tree, look at the real thing more than at your paper.

blocks.name: ydraw-things

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A is a "lollipop tree," drawn from memory. B is drawn from a real tree, with a crooked trunk, branches and bumpy clumps of leaves.

blocks.html: Look, draw a little, look again. Draw what you see, not what you remember.
Our memory keeps a simple picture of things, like a ball on a stick for a tree. Real things are full of surprises: crooked trunks, branches, bumps. Looking shows you the surprises.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Omar is drawing his shoe. What should he notice first?
steps: Big shapes come first.
A shoe is a long, rounded shape with a lower part at the toe.
Small things like laces come last.

blocks.html: Many children draw a tree from memory even when a real tree is in front of them. Keep looking up: how does this tree's trunk bend? Where do the branches go?

blocks.name: ar-shapes
blocks.cap: Looking closely means noticing parts: how many eyes, ears and wings, and what shapes they are.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Put a cup or a toy in front of you. Look at it, draw a little, then look again.

blocks.cap: Draw something real.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Set one object on the table and draw it together, side by side. Every so often, say "Look up!" and point to a part of the object you both missed.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work)

blocks.html: Before you draw, count. How many legs does a spider have? How many petals does this flower have? How many windows does this house have? Counting helps your drawing get the details right.

blocks.name: ydraw-things

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A spider has 8 legs, an ant has 6, this starfish has 5 arms, and a hand has 5 fingers, counting the thumb.

blocks.html: Count first, then draw the right number.
People notice when a number is wrong: a hand with seven fingers looks strange right away. Counting is a quick way to look closely.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: How many legs does a spider have?
steps: Count the legs on each side: four and four.

blocks.html: Many children guess the number: a spider with six legs, a hand with seven fingers. Count on the real thing, or on a picture, before you draw.

blocks.name: ydraw-things
blocks.cap: Spider A has 8 legs. Spider B has only 6.

blocks.name: ydraw-things
blocks.cap: Count the spots, the petals and the round parts.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Look at your own hand. Count the fingers, then draw it.

blocks.cap: Draw your hand.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Touch-and-count is a math skill too: point to each thing once while saying the numbers. The Math Ladder's Touch and Count practices it.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work)

blocks.html: Things feel different: a cat is fuzzy, sand is grainy, water is smooth, bark is rough. In a drawing, the kind of marks you make can show how something feels. This is called texture.

blocks.name: ar-marks

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Marks for fur, sand, water, wood, bricks and grass.

blocks.html: Short strokes for fur, dots for sand, long smooth lines for water, wavy lines for wood.
Our eyes remember how things feel. When a drawing uses fur-like marks, we can almost feel the fur, even though the paper is flat.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: What marks would you use for a sandy beach?
steps: Sand is made of tiny grains.
Tiny dots look like grains.

blocks.html: Some children color everything the same flat way. Try different marks for different things: short lines on the cat, wavy lines on the tree, dots on the path.

blocks.name: ar-sort
blocks.cap: How does each one feel?

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Fill each box with a different texture: fur, dots, wavy lines.

blocks.cap: Make a texture sampler.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Make crayon rubbings: put paper over a leaf, a coin or a bumpy placemat and rub the side of a crayon over it. Then ask your child to draw those textures with marks.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: When the sun shines on a tree, the tree blocks some of the light. That makes a dark patch on the ground: a shadow. The shadow falls on the side away from the sun.

blocks.name: ar-shade

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: The sun is on the left, so the shadow falls to the right.

blocks.html: A shadow falls on the side away from the light.
Light travels in straight lines. The tree stops the light, so the ground behind the tree, on the far side from the sun, stays darker.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: A lamp is on the right side of a cup. Where does the cup's shadow fall?
steps: The light comes from the right.
The shadow falls away from the light.

blocks.html: Many children put the shadow on the same side as the sun. Find the sun first, then put the shadow on the other side.

blocks.name: ar-shade
blocks.cap: The sun is on the right, so the ball's shadow falls to the left.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. In a dark room, shine a flashlight on a toy from one side, then the other. Let your child point to the shadow each time and say where the light is.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Artists use many tools. Crayons, pencils and markers make lines. Paint and brushes spread color. Clay can be squeezed into shapes. Scissors and glue turn paper into pictures.

blocks.name: ydraw-things

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Nine art tools.

blocks.html: Each tool makes a different kind of art. Art is not only crayons and paper.
A pencil line can be erased. Paint can cover a big sky fast. Clay can stand up on the table. Choosing the right tool helps you make what you imagine.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Ruby wants to make a little bowl she can hold. Which tool should she use?
steps: A bowl is solid, not flat.
Clay can be squeezed and shaped with your hands.

blocks.html: Some children think art means only crayons on paper. Clay animals, paper cutouts glued into a collage, and paintings are all art.

blocks.name: ar-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the tools by what they do.

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Choose a tool on the pad: try the pencil color, then a bright color, then the eraser.

blocks.cap: Try the drawing pad's tools.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Set out two or three materials (crayons, a lump of play dough, paper and child-safe scissors) and let your child make the same animal with each. Talk about which was easiest and why.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)

blocks.html: Pictures come in kinds. A portrait shows a person. A landscape shows land and sky: hills, trees, rivers. A still life shows things set on a table, like fruit, flowers or a jug.

blocks.name: ar-shapes

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: A portrait, a landscape and a still life.

blocks.html: Portrait: a person. Landscape: land and sky. Still life: things on a table.
Knowing the kinds helps you talk about art. In a museum, you can say, "This one is a portrait," and look for what the artist shows about the person.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Mona Lisa, by Leonardo da Vinci, is one of the most famous portraits in the world. It hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: A painting shows apples and a jug on a table. What kind of picture is it?
steps: There are no people and no outdoor view.
Things set on a table make a still life.

blocks.html: Some children call any picture with a person in it a portrait. A portrait is about the person. A big outdoor scene with tiny people far away is a landscape.

blocks.name: ar-sort

cards.text: a girl in a red hat

blocks.cap: Sort the pictures.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Look through a picture book or a museum website together and sort what you see: "portrait, landscape or still life?" Some pictures mix kinds; that is fine to talk about.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Responding: perceive and analyze artistic work)

blocks.html: A drawing or a painting is flat: it lies on paper or canvas. A sculpture is solid: it takes up space, and you can walk around it and see its back.

blocks.name: ydraw-things

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child point to the answer, then talk about why.

blocks.cap: Two flat pictures and four sculptures.

blocks.html: Pictures are flat. Sculptures are solid: they have a front, sides and a back.
Sculptors carve stone or wood, shape clay, or put pieces together. Their art has height, width and depth, like a real thing.

blocks.title: Let's look
blocks.q: Hana built a snowman. Is it a picture or a sculpture?
steps: A snowman is solid.
You can walk all the way around it.

blocks.html: Some children think a sculpture must be a statue of a person. A clay bowl, a carved animal, a sandcastle and a stack of metal shapes are sculptures too.

blocks.name: ar-sort
blocks.cap: Sort the art: flat or solid?

blocks.name: ar-canvas

opts.task: Draw a sculpture you would like to make. Then try making it with clay or play dough.

blocks.cap: Plan a sculpture.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Make a small sculpture together from play dough or foil, then turn it around and look at every side. The Math Ladder's Flat and Solid Shapes uses the same idea for shapes.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, Kindergarten to Grade 2 (Creating: generate and organize artistic ideas)
